tips.title: Four polymers, four monomers
tips.body: Protein ← **amino acids**. Starch ← **glucose**. Cellulose ← **glucose**. DNA ← **nucleotides**. Naming the monomer is what the spec actually asks for, and starch and cellulose sharing one is the fact questions are built on.

tips.title: Be exact about DNA
tips.body: **Two** chains, **four** different nucleotides, a **double helix**, and it **encodes genetic instructions**. Those are four separate marks — an answer saying only *a double helix of nucleotides* has left half of them behind.

tips.title: An amino acid has one of each group
tips.body: –NH₂ at one end, –COOH at the other. That is why it can polymerise **with itself**, while a diol needs a diacid to react with. Two groups is the rule; two *different* groups is what makes amino acids special.

tips.title: Same monomer, different material
tips.body: Starch and cellulose settle it: identical glucose units, completely different properties, because the units are **joined differently**. When asked why two polymers differ, look at the links before you look at the monomer.

tips.title: Add the monomers, then take the water
tips.body: For any condensation product, add the monomers' atoms together and subtract one water **per link formed**. Two glycines minus one H₂O gives C₄H₈N₂O₃ — the same method as for a polyester, on a different molecule.

why.matters:
The molecules that living things are built from are polymers, made in exactly the way the last topic described: monomers joining, a small molecule lost at each link. A protein is not a different kind of chemistry from nylon.

What is different is the **choosing**. An addition polymer repeats one monomer; a protein picks from twenty in a particular order, and DNA from four. The order is the information, which is how a chain of atoms comes to carry instructions.

examples.title: Paper and potatoes are the same monomer
examples.body:
Starch and cellulose are both polymers of **glucose** — the same small molecule, joined up in enormous numbers. One is what a potato stores its energy in; the other is the fibre that holds a tree upright and the stuff a sheet of paper is made of.

The difference is how the glucose units are turned as they join, which lets cellulose chains lie alongside each other and grip. And it is why you can digest a potato and not a newspaper: the enzyme that takes starch apart does not fit the other arrangement.

examples.title: Four polymers, and what they are made of
examples.body:
Everything alive is largely built from four polymers, and each has its own kind of monomer. Knowing which goes with which is worth a mark on its own, and it also makes the rest of the topic make sense.

Two of them share a monomer entirely. Starch and cellulose are both glucose, which is the clearest evidence in the course that **how** a polymer is put together matters as much as what it is put together from.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading polymers of living things: protein made from amino acids, starch and cellulose both made from glucose, and DNA made from nucleotides

examples.title: Why four letters is enough
examples.body:
DNA is built from only **four** different monomers. That sounds far too few to carry the instructions for an animal, until you notice that the information is in the **order** rather than in the variety.

A protein has twenty amino acids to choose from and an English sentence has twenty-six letters, and neither is obviously richer than the other. Length does the work: a short alphabet and a long chain carry as much as you like. DNA also keeps **two** chains wound into a double helix, so the message is written down twice.

steps.title: Polymers that living things make
steps.body:
Not every polymer comes from a factory. Some of the most important molecules in living things are polymers, and they are built in exactly the way the last topic described: small monomers joining, with a small molecule lost each time.

Four matter here, and for each you should be able to **name the monomer it is made from** — the table below gives all four.

Starch and cellulose are both made from glucose, yet they are very different materials — one is a food store and the other is the fibre that makes up plant cell walls. The same monomer joined in a different way gives a different polymer, which is a good illustration of how much the arrangement matters.

All of these are formed by **condensation** polymerisation, losing water as the links form.

steps.title: Amino acids
steps.body:
This section is **Higher tier only**.

An **amino acid** has **two different functional groups** in the same molecule:

- an **amino group, –NH₂**
- a **carboxyl group, –COOH** — the carboxylic acid group from two topics ago

That is the whole reason amino acids polymerise. The last topic's rule was that condensation needs **two functional groups per monomer**, one at each end, so the chain can grow both ways. Amino acids satisfy it — but with **two different** groups rather than two of the same.

The spec names **glycine**, **H₂NCH₂COOH**. You can see both groups in that formula: the H₂N at the front and the COOH at the end, with a CH₂ between them.

When amino acids join, the **–NH₂** of one reacts with the **–COOH** of the next, a **water molecule is lost**, and the chain grows. The product is a **polypeptide**.

Because the two groups are different, an amino acid can join to another amino acid **at either end**, and **different amino acids can be combined in the same chain**. Chains built from different amino acids in different orders are **proteins** — and that variety is where all the different proteins in a body come from.

steps.title: DNA
steps.body:
**DNA** — deoxyribonucleic acid — is a **large molecule essential for life**. It **encodes the genetic instructions** for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

The structure is worth stating precisely, because each part is a separate mark:

- **Most DNA molecules are two polymer chains.** Not one.
- They are made from **four different monomers called nucleotides**.
- The two chains are wound into a **double helix**.

The number **four** matters. Every one of the enormous variety of genetic instructions is written using only four different monomers — what changes is the **order** they come in. A very long chain of four possible units can encode an extraordinary amount of information, in the same way that a long enough sequence of letters can write any book.

That is the same principle as proteins, where a limited set of amino acids in different orders gives every protein in the body. **Order carries the information**, in both cases.

steps.title: Starch and cellulose: the same monomer, twice
steps.body:
**Starch** and **cellulose** are both polymers of **glucose**. Yet starch is a soft energy store and cellulose is the tough fibre in plant cell walls, strong enough to hold a tree up.

How can the same monomer give such different materials? Because the glucose units are **joined differently**. The arrangement of the links changes how the chains sit together, and that changes everything about the material:

- In **cellulose**, the chains lie straight and alongside each other, so they pack tightly and hold together strongly — giving **strong fibres**.
- In **starch**, the chains coil, which makes a compact store that is easy to break down again when the plant needs the energy.

This is a useful general point, and it is the reason the spec puts these two side by side: **a polymer's properties depend on how the monomers are joined, not only on what they are.** The same idea explained why poly(ethene) is flexible while other addition polymers are rigid.

Humans can digest starch but not cellulose, which is why cellulose passes through as dietary fibre — the enzymes that break the links in starch do not fit the links in cellulose.

steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the monomer of each: protein, starch, cellulose, DNA.

3. How many different monomers are there in DNA, and how many chains in most DNA molecules?

**Part B.**

**Part C — Higher tier.**

7. Explain why amino acids can undergo condensation polymerisation, referring to the rule about functional groups.
8. Two glycine molecules join. Work out the formula of the dipeptide formed, given that glycine is C₂H₅NO₂ and one water molecule is lost.

steps.title: Going deeper: why order carries information
steps.body:
**The same principle twice.** Proteins and DNA both work the same way, and noticing that is what a top answer does.

- **DNA** uses **four** different nucleotides. The **order** along the chain encodes the instructions.
- **Proteins** are chains of **different amino acids**, and again the **order** decides which protein it is and what it does.

In both cases the number of possible sequences grows enormously with length. A chain of 10 units chosen from 4 has over a million possible sequences; a real DNA molecule is millions of units long. So a **small alphabet and a long chain** is all that is needed, which is why life does not need hundreds of different monomers.

**Natural polymers are condensation polymers.** Proteins, starch, cellulose and DNA are all made by joining monomers with the loss of water. That connects this topic to the last one: the same chemistry, in a cell rather than a reactor. And it means the rule carries over — count the atoms, and the repeating unit has **fewer** than the monomers did between them.

**Why amino acids are unusual.** The polyester in the last topic needed **two different monomers**, because each one had two of the **same** group — a diol could only react with a diacid. An amino acid has **one of each group in the same molecule**, so it can polymerise **with itself**. That is why a protein can be built from a single kind of amino acid repeated, or from many different ones mixed in any order — a flexibility the polyester does not have.

**Structure decides properties, monomer alone does not.** Starch and cellulose make the point unanswerable: identical monomers, completely different materials. So when a question asks why two polymers differ, *they are made of different things* is rarely the whole answer. Ask how the chains are **joined** and how they **sit together**.

**Be exact about DNA.** *Two* chains, *four* monomers, a *double helix*, and it *encodes genetic instructions*. Each is a separate mark and each is easy to blur — saying DNA is *a double helix made of nucleotides* leaves two of the four marks on the table.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Protein** is made from **amino acids**; **starch** and **cellulose** from **glucose**; **DNA** from **nucleotides**.
- All are **condensation** polymers, losing water as the links form.
- **Higher tier — amino acids** have **two different** functional groups: **–NH₂** and **–COOH**.
- The spec's example is **glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH**.
- The –NH₂ of one reacts with the –COOH of the next, losing **water**, to give a **polypeptide**.
- **Different amino acids in one chain give proteins.**
- **DNA** is **deoxyribonucleic acid**, a large molecule **essential for life**.
- It **encodes the genetic instructions** for development and functioning in organisms and viruses.
- Most DNA molecules are **two polymer chains** of **four different nucleotides**, in a **double helix**.
- **Starch and cellulose** share a monomer but differ because the units are **joined differently**.
- A polymer's properties depend on **how** the monomers are joined, not only on what they are.
- In both DNA and proteins, the **order** of the monomers carries the information.

questions.prompt: Amino acids polymerise to form polypeptides. Name the two functional groups in an amino acid, explain why having both allows polymerisation, and describe what happens when two amino acids join.
questions.solution: An amino acid contains an amino group, N H two, and a carboxyl group, C O O H. These are two different functional groups, and the molecule has one of each. Condensation polymerisation requires each monomer to have two functional groups so that the chain can grow at both ends, and an amino acid meets this requirement. Because it carries one of each group rather than two of the same, an amino acid can react with another amino acid directly, unlike a diol which must react with a dicarboxylic acid. When two amino acids join, the amino group of one reacts with the carboxyl group of the other, a molecule of water is lost, and a link is formed between them. Many amino acids joined in this way form a polypeptide, and when different amino acids are combined in the same chain the result is a protein.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The two groups.** An **amino** group, **–NH₂**, and a **carboxyl** group, **–COOH**. In glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, you can see both: the H₂N at the front, the COOH at the end.

**Why both are needed.** Condensation polymerisation requires **two functional groups per monomer**, so the chain can grow at **both** ends. An amino acid has exactly that.

What makes it unusual is that it has **one of each** rather than two of the same. A diol has two –OH groups and so must react with a **different** monomer, a diacid. An amino acid can react with **another amino acid** directly.

**When two join.** The **–NH₂** of one reacts with the **–COOH** of the other, a molecule of **water is lost**, and a link forms.

**The product.** Many amino acids joined this way give a **polypeptide**. When **different** amino acids are combined in the same chain, the result is a **protein** — and the order they come in is what makes one protein different from another.

questions.prompt: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet starch is an energy store and cellulose forms strong plant fibres. Explain how two polymers of the same monomer can have such different properties, and why humans can digest one but not the other.
questions.solution: Starch and cellulose are made from the same monomer, glucose, so the difference between them cannot come from the monomer itself. The difference comes from the way the glucose units are joined together. In cellulose the chains are straight and lie alongside one another so that they pack closely and are held together strongly, which produces strong fibres suitable for plant cell walls. In starch the chains are coiled, which makes a compact store that can be broken down easily when the plant needs energy. This shows that the properties of a polymer depend on how the monomers are joined and how the chains sit together, not only on which monomer is used. Another example is that our digestive enzymes can break the links in starch but not the different links in cellulose, which is why cellulose passes through the body as dietary fibre.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Start from what is the same.** Both are polymers of **glucose**, so the difference cannot come from the monomer.

**The actual reason.** The glucose units are **joined differently**, and that changes how the chains sit together:

- In **cellulose**, the chains lie **straight and alongside each other**, so they pack closely and hold together strongly — **strong fibres**, which is what a cell wall needs.
- In **starch**, the chains **coil**, giving a compact store that is easily broken down when energy is needed.

**The general point.** A polymer's properties depend on **how the monomers are joined** and how the chains pack, not only on which monomer was used.

**Another example.** Human digestive enzymes break the links in starch but not the different links in cellulose, which is why cellulose passes through as **dietary fibre**. The molecules are made of the same units; only the links differ.

The structure of this answer is worth copying: say what is the same, rule it out as the cause, then give the real reason.

examTechnique.body:
Learn the four polymers with their monomers as pairs, and note that starch and cellulose share one.

For DNA, give every part of the description that is asked for: two chains, four nucleotides, a double helix, and that it encodes genetic instructions. Each is a separate mark.

For amino acids, name both functional groups and say they are different from each other, then explain that two groups are what allow a chain to grow at both ends.

When working out the product of a condensation, add the monomers and subtract one water for each link.

When asked why two polymers of the same monomer differ, say what is the same first, then give the real reason: the units are joined differently.

Do not describe natural polymers as addition polymers. They all lose water as they form.
examinerErrors: Saying DNA is made of amino acids rather than nucleotides.
Giving the number of DNA monomers as two rather than four.
Describing DNA as a single chain.
Saying starch and cellulose are made from different monomers.
Giving an amino acid two of the same functional group.
Calling protein formation an addition polymerisation.
Forgetting to subtract the water when working out a dipeptide formula.
Explaining the difference between starch and cellulose by saying they contain different elements.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer notices that proteins and DNA work the same way — a small set of monomers whose **order** carries the information — and says so rather than treating them as two unrelated facts. It explains why an amino acid is unusual by comparing it with a diol, which shows the rule about functional groups has been understood rather than memorised. Given starch and cellulose, it states what is the same before explaining what differs, and draws the general conclusion that structure decides properties. On DNA it gives all four facts precisely, because it knows each is marked separately.
